css-unit-converter.quickAnswer: With the default 16 px base font, 16 px = 1 rem, and 10 vw on a 1440 px wide viewport = 144 px. Enter a value, pick from/to units, and set your real base font size and viewport dimensions below - the result recalculates instantly.
keyFacts: rem is relative to the root (html) font size - 16 px by default in browsers.
em is relative to the parent element font size, which makes it compound in nested elements.
% for font-size is relative to the parent font size: 100% = same size.
vw/vh are relative to the viewport: 1 vw = 1% of viewport width.
px is absolute on screen but still scales with browser zoom, so layouts stay usable.
Modern best practice: rem for typography and spacing, px or rem for borders, vw/vh sparingly for full-viewport sections.
howTo: Choose the from-unit and the to-unit (px, rem, em, %, vw, vh).
Set your base font size (default 16) and viewport width/height to match your design.
Read the instant result; swap reverses the conversion.
css-unit-converter.formula:
px value = value × (px per from-unit) ÷ (px per to-unit).
px per unit: px = 1; rem = base font; em = base font; % = base font ÷ 100; vw = viewport width ÷ 100; vh = viewport height ÷ 100.
Example (base 16): 2 rem → px = 2 × 16 ÷ 1 = 32 px.
css-unit-converter.workedExample:
Convert 10 vw to px on a 1440 px wide viewport:
1. px per vw = 1440 ÷ 100 = 14.4 px.
2. 10 × 14.4 = 144 px.
Convert 24 px to rem (base 16):
1. px per rem = 16.
2. 24 × 1 ÷ 16 = 1.5 rem.

faqs.a: By default, 1 rem = 16 px, because browsers set the root font size to 16 px. If the root font size is changed (or the user zooms), rem scales with it. This tool lets you set your own base to match your project.

faqs.q: Should I use px or rem?
faqs.a: Use rem for font sizes, margins and padding so your site respects user font-size settings (accessibility). Use px for hairline borders or pixel-perfect decorative details. Most modern codebases default to rem.

faqs.q: What is the difference between em and rem?
faqs.a: rem is always relative to the root font size; em is relative to the parent element font size. Nested ems compound (1.2 em inside 1.2 em = 1.44×), which surprises people - rem avoids that.

1 vw equals 1% of the viewport (browser window) width. On a 1440 px wide window, 10 vw = 144 px. They are great for full-bleed hero sections but can make text unreadably small or huge, so pair them with clamp() for typography.

faqs.q: Why does my rem math not match the design?
faqs.a: Usually the root font size is not 16 px - many projects set html { font-size: 62.5% } (10 px) or users zoom. Enter your actual base font size in this tool and the numbers will match.

Not exactly - browsers scale px values when users zoom, so px text still zooms. But px ignores the user font-size preference setting, while rem respects it. For body text, rem is the safer, more respectful choice.

mistakes: Assuming the base font is always 16 px — many projects set html to 62.5% (10 px). Enter your real base or every rem conversion is wrong.
Nested ems compound: 1.2 em inside 1.2 em = 1.44×, not 1.2×. That's exactly why rem exists — use it for predictable sizing.
Converting vw without setting your viewport width gives a meaningless number — 10 vw on a 1440 px screen is 144 px, on a 390 px phone it's 39 px.
% means different things in CSS: 100% font-size = parent's size, but 100% width = parent's width. This tool uses the font-size meaning only.
Typing px values 'for precision' on body text ignores users' font-size settings. Use rem for text so accessibility settings still work.
